title: New Ravens QB Jacoby Brissett embraces ‘crash course’ after trade
content:
OWINGS MILLS, Md. — Quarterback Jacoby Brissett has been on seven teams in 11 NFL seasons, but he’s never been through this: joining a team in midseason and having little more than a week to prepare for a game critical to keeping playoff hopes alive.

“It’s definitely a crash course,” Brissett said Thursday in his first comments to reporters since he was acquired by the Baltimore Ravens from the Arizona Cardinals in a trade last week. “No question.

“It’s been a long but fast week or so.”

Brissett, 33, arrived in Baltimore over the weekend and immediately began to immerse himself in the Ravens’ playbook. It has helped that he was with Ravens quarterbacks coach Israel Woolfork in Arizona and Ravens pass game coordinator Marcus Brady in Indianapolis. Brissett, who is barely 11 days removed from starting for the Cardinals against the Dallas Cowboys on Nov. 1, also has an extra day to prepare because the Ravens (4-5) don’t play the winless Los Angeles Chargers until Monday night.

Still, the sense of urgency is high. The Ravens brought in Brissett with the idea that he could stabilize a team that has lost four consecutive games and an offense that has totaled just 43 points during that span. Starting quarterback Lamar Jackson is out indefinitely with a right thumb injury and his backup, Tyler Huntley, will miss the rest of the season because of right toe surgery.

The Ravens started undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano in last Thursday’s 33-10 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars, but the offense was barely functional. Brissett, who was demoted to third-string quarterback in Arizona after he was benched during the Cowboys game, will be tasked with changing that and helping the Ravens stay afloat until Jackson potentially returns late in the regular season.

“We all know he can throw the ball,” said Ravens No. 1 wide receiver Zay Flowers. “He can spin it, but he’s just been connecting with us, telling us how he feels about a route, where we should be, talking to (Derrick Henry) about certain things coming out of the backfield. He’s just letting his experience show.”

Brissett’s first practice with the team was on Wednesday. He stayed on the field well after practice Wednesday and Thursday for individual work with Flowers and other wide receivers.

“It’s hard for me to say what type of impact (I can have) until it shows,” Brissett said. “I’m really just coming out, trying to do my job to the best of my ability, be a good teammate, keep things simple (and) not try to overcomplicate this thing right now. … Just excited for this opportunity and trying to make the most of it.”

Brissett, who has started 20 games over the past two years with Arizona, had a solid season in 2025, completing just under 65 percent of his passes for 3,366 yards, 23 touchdowns and eight interceptions. The New England Patriots’ 2016 third-round pick stayed away from the Cardinals facility for much of the offseason because he wanted a contract more in line with his status as the team’s starter.

He ultimately agreed to a reworked one-year, $15.5 million deal in July, but this season has been a struggle. He averaged just 5.6 yards per attempt and was intercepted seven times in parts of eight games.

With him and the Cardinals’ offense struggling against Dallas, coach Mike LaFleur turned to fellow veteran Gardner Minshew, who led a comeback win. However, a week later Minshew sustained a season-ending elbow injury, while Brissett was already in Baltimore, getting ready for his next opportunity.

“It was obviously a tough situation,” Brissett said. “Then you get the news like the next day or two … and then you kind of have to get your mind wrapped around another situation. So, it’s kind of all over the place, but having those extra days kind of helped me settle my emotions down and then obviously refocusing and figuring out what the next steps were. Then, getting here and figuring out that I’m going to be here and figuring out how to attack this situation.”
